4) We'll set up a staging key and a sample routing policy so calls from your staging cluster route to a staging Redwood pool.

1) For service-to-service, are you recommending long-lived API keys stored in our vault + occasional rotation, or short-lived JWTs minted by our KMS for every service-to-service request? Our infra prefers short-lived where possible but we need guidance on tradeoffs.

2) Can the Redwood SDK automatically refresh tokens (i.e., handle exchange of a long-lived service key for short-lived session tokens)? If so, what auth flows are supported (OAuth client_credentials / JWT-bearer / signed headers)?

3) For embeddings/reranker calls: any best practices for isolation of keys/usage quotas (e.g., separate keys per model or per service)? We want to avoid a noisy neighbor service exhausting embeddings quota for others.

4) For audit logging: we need per-key/token audit trails (who used which key, when). Does Redwood surface those in Console or do we need to pipe logs to our SIEM?

Samir / team — thanks for the clear questions. Below are concise answers and recommended PoC config. Happy to expand during the sync on Wed.

1) Short-lived JWTs vs long-lived API keys
- Recommendation: Use a hybrid approach for the PoC.
  - Create a service account per FintechCo service (recommended) and issue a long-lived service key stored in your vault (rotated on a cadence).
  - At runtime, the service exchanges the long-lived service key for a short-lived JWT (default TTL 15 minutes) signed by Redwood or minted via your KMS (we support both workflows). 
  - Tradeoffs: long-lived keys are simpler but require robust rotation/ALM; short-lived JWTs reduce blast radius and are preferred for high-security environments.

2) SDK refresh & supported flows
- Redwood SDKs (Node/Python/Go) include an optional token-refresh helper. Two main flows we support:
  a) client_credentials (OAuth2) — for customers who prefer OAuth2 client_id/client_secret exchange.
  b) JWT-bearer / signed-token exchange — service uses a long-lived private key or vault-stored secret to request short-lived JWTs from Redwood.
- The SDK can perform automatic refresh by calling the /v1/auth/refresh endpoint and caching tokens; we provide examples in the attached README.

3) Embeddings / reranker isolation and quotas
- Best practice: create separate API keys (or service accounts) per logical workload. Example: a /nlp/embeddings service and a /search/ranker service with distinct keys and quotas.
- If you use routing policies, you can map a prefix (e.g., X-Redwood-Route: embeddings) to a dedicated pool and model variant to prevent noisy neighbor effects.
- We also support per-key quotas and rate limits configured in Console; we’ll pre-configure rate limits for the PoC.

4) Audit logging and SIEM integration
- Audit trails: Console surfaces per-key/token activity with timestamp, route, and request id.
- For deeper retention / SIEM: you can ship request-level logs to your logging endpoint (we support syslog / HTTPS ingestion) or forward via a Log Export to your Splunk/Datadog.

PoC config (recommended):
- Create three service accounts: staging-embeddings, staging-ranker, prod-proxy.
- Use long-lived keys stored in your vault and set rotation at 90 days for now. For prod we recommend automated rotation (30 days) + short-lived JWTs for all server traffic.
- Enable per-key quotas: 10k embedding units/day for staging-embeddings; 5k/day for staging-ranker.
- Routing: set a header-based routing policy (X-Env: staging/prod) to direct staging traffic to the staging pool.

Attachments: I attached the integration-checklist with the sample SDK snippets and a short README showing the token exchange flow.
